explanations.explanation: Right in God's hands, baker. The Teacher says "the righteous and the wise, as well as their deeds, are in God’s hands." That covers the people and their deeds. I think that's a comfort, because nobody has to hold it all together alone.

I get the guess, since the Teacher is a king himself (Ecclesiastes 1:1). But he doesn't hand the righteous and the wise over to any king. He says they and their deeds are in God's hands. That's a king pointing higher than his own crown, and it takes some humility.

We all like to think we hold the steering wheel. The Teacher says the righteous and the wise, and their deeds, are in God's hands instead. I used to think I steered everything too, right up until I landed in the back of a junk drawer. Turns out Someone bigger was holding the whole thing.

It's the other way around, friend. The Teacher says "Man does not know what lies ahead, whether love or hate." Nobody gets a peek at the forecast. I bake for a living and I still can't tell you how a batch will turn out until the oven opens.

False is right. The Teacher says "Man does not know what lies ahead, whether love or hate." Nobody gets a crystal ball, not the righteous and not the wise. I can't even call a batch before it comes out, and I've got a window on my oven.

A common fate, yes. The Teacher says "There is a common fate for the righteous and the wicked, for the good and the bad…" Then he keeps stacking pairs: clean and unclean, the one who sacrifices and the one who does not. It's a hard list, and he doesn't sugarcoat a single pair.

That's a fair thing to expect, but it isn't what this verse says. He says "There is a common fate for the righteous and the wicked…" One fate reaches both sides of every pair. Hold onto that, because it's the whole point of this stretch.

explanations.answer: They all answer to the king
explanations.explanation: The writer is a king, so I see why the king came to mind. But he never says they answer to him. He says "There is a common fate for the righteous and the wicked…" Same fate, no ranking.
True. The Teacher says "the hearts of men are full of evil and madness while they are alive." That's a hard line, and he doesn't dress it up. I think it's why he turns to hope in the very next verse.

It's actually true, and I understand the second guess. The Teacher says "the hearts of men are full of evil and madness while they are alive, and afterward they join the dead." He's being blunt here, not gentle. That bluntness is also why the hope in the next verse hits so hard.

True. The Teacher says "even a live dog is better than a dead lion." The lion is the famous fierce one, and the dog is just a dog. Still, the one that's breathing wins. He's backing up the hope he just gave to anyone among the living.

It's actually true. The Teacher says "even a live dog is better than a dead lion." Picture the fiercest lion next to the scruffiest dog, and the living one comes out ahead. That's him showing there is hope for anyone among the living. Wild picture, but that's the verse.

That they will die. The Teacher says "For the living know that they will die, but the dead know nothing." It's an odd thing to call an advantage, but he sets it right beside the hope of the living. I think knowing it means the living still have time to use.

Tempting, but the Teacher says in verse 12 that "no man knows his time." The living know they will die, just not when. It's like knowing the cookies will finish, but your timer is broken. I'd take a working timer any day.

He never says that here. The living know "that they will die," and that's the whole list. He goes on to say there is no work in Sheol (Ecclesiastes 9:10). Nothing in this stretch promises the work will last.

explanations.answer: The memory of them is forgotten
explanations.explanation: That's the reason he gives. The Teacher says "They have no further reward, because the memory of them is forgotten." It's a heavy line, and he states it plainly. He doesn't say any more about it than that.

Unfinished work sounds sensible, and I've left plenty of dough half stamped myself. But that's not the reason he gives. He says "because the memory of them is forgotten." The text gives forgetting as the reason, not unfinished work.

Judgment is a big word, and I see why it came to mind. But the Teacher doesn't give that reason here. He says they have no further reward "because the memory of them is forgotten." Let's stick to what he actually says, baker.

True. The Teacher says "Their love, their hate, and their envy have already vanished, and they will never again have a share in all that is done under the sun." It's a short list and a blunt one. I think he's showing how different things are for the living.

That one is actually true. Verse 6 says "Their love, their hate, and their envy have already vanished, and they will never again have a share in all that is done under the sun." Three feelings, all gone together. He keeps it plain and adds nothing to it.

explanations.answer: God has already approved your works
explanations.explanation: That's his reason. The bread and the wine come with a cheerful heart because God has already approved your works. Notice the order: the approval comes first, and the enjoying follows. Eating with joy is about the easiest job in my bakery, and I've had a lot of practice.

explanations.answer: Your labor has finally come to an end
explanations.explanation: The labor isn't over in this passage. Two verses later he is still talking about "your labor under the sun" (Ecclesiastes 9:9). The reason he gives is that God has already approved your works. So the bread and wine are for right in the middle of the work.

explanations.answer: Your enemies have all run away
explanations.explanation: No enemies show up anywhere in this passage. The reason he gives is that God has already approved your works. All the Teacher puts on the table is bread, wine and a cheerful heart. Honestly, I'd settle for the crumbs staying off the floor.
Your beloved wife. The Teacher says "Enjoy life with your beloved wife…" He means it for all your fleeting days. Notice the word is enjoy life, not just get through it.

I get why kids came to mind, since I think about my own six cookie cutter kids all the time. But the verse says to enjoy life with "your beloved wife." Sons and daughters aren't mentioned in it. We'll stick to what the Teacher says.
Friends are great company, and I still think about the ones from my old junk drawer days. But this verse names someone else: "your beloved wife." Friends aren't in it. Good guess, though.

It's the opposite, friend. The Teacher calls it "the fleeting life that God has given you under the sun" and says "all your fleeting days." Fleeting means quick, not long and lasting. Think of a fresh batch on the counter with a crowd around.

False is right. The Teacher says "the fleeting life that God has given you under the sun" and "all your fleeting days." He calls it quick, not long and lasting. I think that's why the verse starts with the word enjoy.
All your might. The Teacher says "Whatever you find to do with your hands, do it with all your might." That means full effort, no coasting. When I stamp a cookie, my mustache and I are all in.
Caution has its place, but that's not the word he uses. The Teacher says to do it "with all your might." No holding back. A very cautious stamper makes a very faint cookie.
Patience is a good thing, but it isn't what this verse asks for. The Teacher says "do it with all your might." That's full effort. I'm patient by trade, and even I lean my whole weight on the stamp.

explanations.answer: In Sheol there is no work
explanations.explanation: That's his reason. He says to work with all your might "for in Sheol, where you are going, there is no work or planning or knowledge or wisdom." Sheol is where the dead go. I think it tells us the time for work is the time we have right now.

Harvest is a good picture, but it isn't the one he uses. The Teacher's reason is that in Sheol there is "no work or planning or knowledge or wisdom." No harvest shows up in this passage. His reason is about where you are going.

That sounds like something from a proverb, but it isn't in this passage. The Teacher says to work with all your might "for in Sheol, where you are going, there is no work or planning or knowledge or wisdom." Poverty never comes up here. His reason is Sheol.

True. The Teacher says "The race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong." The fastest runner doesn't always take the prize, and the strongest fighter doesn't always win. He's about to say the same thing about bread, wealth and favor.

It's actually true. The Teacher says "The race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong." Fast legs and big muscles come with no guarantee. He says it before he moves on to bread, wealth and favor.

explanations.answer: Time and chance happen to all
explanations.explanation: That's the reason. The Teacher says "For time and chance happen to all." You can plan the whole batch and still have the power flicker. Swift or slow, strong or not, it reaches everybody.

That's a true line from Scripture: "Humble yourselves before the Lord, and He will exalt you." (James 4:10) But it isn't the reason in this verse. The Teacher says the race isn't to the swift because "time and chance happen to all." Good thought, different verse.

Tired muscles are a fair guess, and my mustache wears out after a long day of packing boxes. But the Teacher gives a different reason. He says "For time and chance happen to all." Nothing about anyone getting tired.

explanations.answer: Fish caught in a cruel net
explanations.explanation: Fish in a cruel net. The Teacher says men are ensnared "Like fish caught in a cruel net or birds trapped in a snare." Two pictures, and in both the catch happens without warning. He says the evil time "suddenly falls upon them."

Sheep show up in plenty of Bible pictures, but not in this one. Here the Teacher says men are like fish caught in a cruel net or birds trapped in a snare. Both are caught in a moment. Good guess, wrong flock.

Chaff is a strong picture, but the Teacher doesn't use it here. He says men are ensnared "Like fish caught in a cruel net or birds trapped in a snare." Being caught is the whole idea. Nothing in this verse gets blown away.
